# Limitations {#sec-limitations}

Every behavioural quantity in this paper is a share of conversations matched to tasks (@sec-data). It describes usage of one assistant on one platform, not the conduct of the people employed in an occupation. A high automation share for an occupation's tasks says that the conversations classified to those tasks were mostly of the automation kind; it says nothing about how many of the people in that occupation use the model, or how they divide their own work. The wording rule applied throughout is therefore a substantive limit on what the results can claim. It binds RQ1 most, where H1–H4 relate usage shares to occupational wages, education, error costs and country income (@sec-rq1): the regressors describe occupations and countries, while the outcome describes only the conversations that reached the platform from them. Usage is also concentrated. In a post-result diagnostic (PAP §11 D-3; exploratory; not a decision), leaving out SOC major group {{< var diag.h1.leave_out_soc_major_15.dropped >}}, which carries {{< var diag.h1.leave_out_soc_major_15.dropped_weight_pct >}}% of the H1 weight, gives $\beta_w$ = {{< var diag.h1.leave_out_soc_major_15.beta_w >}} (p = {{< var diag.h1.leave_out_soc_major_15.p_w >}}) and $\beta_e$ = {{< var diag.h1.leave_out_soc_major_15.beta_e >}} (p = {{< var diag.h1.leave_out_soc_major_15.p_e >}}) (@tbl-diag-h1-influence). The robustness rows that move the H1 coefficients most, R26 `gwa` and `dwa`, R24 r4 and r5, R24 `r6_1p_api` and R10 `ub`, are reported in @sec-robustness.

No AEI release names the model that classifies its conversations, and the platform scope widens across releases (@tbl-regimes). A change in the classifier, or in the population of conversations it sees, between two releases cannot be distinguished from a change in how people work with the model. This is the first open risk of the data audit, and the published files cannot resolve it (@sec-data). It bears on every comparison across releases: on H2 above all (below), and on the exploratory, look-ahead `A_pooled` index, which averages releases measured under different regimes (@sec-rq2).

Suppression enters at two levels. Within published tasks, AEI withholds cells below its thresholds; the primary measure renormalises over the classified patterns, and the R10 bounds count the suppressed mass as all automation or as none. Across occupations, the width of those bounds on the automation share has a median of {{< var rq2.bounds_occupation.automation.p50 >}} pp and an interquartile range of {{< var rq2.bounds_occupation.automation.p25 >}} to {{< var rq2.bounds_occupation.automation.p75 >}} pp over {{< var rq2.bounds_occupation.automation.n >}} occupations (@tbl-rq2-bounds-occupations). Occupations with no AEI usage are a separate case: they are unpublished in AEI, not measured as zero, and are assigned zero by assumption (D3). Under Design B this covers {{< var audit.zero_assigned_pct.b >}}% of employment (@sec-data). The RQ2 correlations depend on that assumption, and R3, which drops those occupations instead, lowers them most (@sec-rq2).

{{< include _generated/tables/rq2-bounds-occupations.md >}}

Two further construction choices are equal splits that use no employment information. A task statement shared by several occupations gives each an equal part of its usage (D4). This keeps the numerator of the usage index independent of its employment denominator, but it produces dispersion in usage within groups of related occupations that share tasks, which the data audit lists among its open risks (@sec-data). The pre-registered alternative, R11, splits in proportion to employment and so equalises usage across the occupations sharing a task by construction; it removes the dispersion rather than measuring how much of it is an artefact (@sec-robustness). Likewise, the NAICS to SIC to FF49 concordance splits a NAICS code equally over the SIC codes it maps to (D23), so the industry weights are structural rather than employment-based, a departure from the design spec's employment-weighted crosswalk that PAP §10.2 records. R33 is the employment-weighted row (@sec-robustness). The same OEWS occupation-to-industry weights enter both sides of every RQ2 comparison, so part of each correlation is common occupational mix (@sec-rq2).

The time dimension of H2 is four release cross-sections, r2 to r5 (@sec-methods). Under task fixed effects the trend is identified only across releases, so its effective time degrees of freedom are few, which is why the release-level wild bootstrap is a co-condition. Measured within-task automation rises by {{< var rq1.h2.beta >}} pp per year (interval {{< var rq1.h2.trend.ci_low >}} to {{< var rq1.h2.trend.ci_high >}}; task-clustered p {{< var rq1.h2.p_cluster >}}; release-level wild-bootstrap p = {{< var rq1.h2.p_wild >}}), and H2 is {{< var rq1.h2.decision_text >}}: the release-level co-condition fails at {{< var rq1.holm.h2 >}} (@sec-rq1). The rise is one r2 to r3 step of {{< var rq1.h2.release_effect.r3.estimate >}} pp followed by a fall, to {{< var rq1.h2.release_effect.r4.estimate >}} and {{< var rq1.h2.release_effect.r5.estimate >}} pp relative to r2 (@fig-rq1-h2-release-effects). Leaving out r2 reverses the sign of β, to {{< var diag.h2.leave_out_release_r2.beta >}} pp per year, in the post-result diagnostic of PAP §11 D-3 (exploratory; not a decision; @tbl-diag-h2-influence). The r2 to r3 step coincides with the change in the classified-conversation base, so classifier or platform drift cannot be separated from behaviour, and R22 `api_r3_r5` and R23 run the other way (@sec-robustness). The balanced panel removes {{< var diag.h2.balancing_removed.n_tasks >}} tasks carrying {{< var diag.h2.balancing_removed.usage_share_pct >}}% of usage (descriptive; @tbl-diag-h2-influence).

The market test is a cross-section of {{< var design.n_industries >}} FF49 industries, and one of them dominates it. Design B delegation exposure places {{< var audit.exposure.b.z_del_max_industry >}} at {{< var audit.exposure.b.z_del_max >}} SD, against {{< var audit.exposure.b.z_del_2nd >}} SD for the next industry, and Softw's leverage is {{< var rq3.influence.softw.h5.leverage >}} in the H5 regression and {{< var rq3.influence.softw.h5b.leverage >}} in H5b (@tbl-rq3-influence-softw). Softw thus sits far from the rest of the cross-section in exposure, although its DFBETAS and Cook's distance on the slope are small and the R13 estimates lie close to the primaries (@sec-markets). The ranked (R12) and drop-Softw (R13) specifications are co-primary for this reason, and dropping Softw raises the MDE from {{< var rq3.h5.mde >}} to {{< var rq3.h5.mde_r13 >}} pp per standard deviation for H5 and from {{< var rq3.h5b.mde >}} to {{< var rq3.h5b.mde_r13 >}} for H5b (@sec-markets).

The confirmatory returns span one window, {{< var design.window.start >}} to {{< var design.window.end >}}, of {{< var design.window.months >}} months: a single draw of the cross-section of industry alphas. For that window the H5 MDE of {{< var d11.primary_mde >}} pp per standard deviation exceeds the plausibility threshold of {{< var design.plausibility_pp >}} pp, so the D11 rule applies and the market results are read as a statement about what this window can detect (@sec-markets). The MDE equals {{< var power.mde_over_s >}} times s, the spread of historical slopes across windows (@sec-methods).

Design B is out of sample in its AEI data only, not strictly real-time (S1). Its OEWS {{< var vintage.oews.primary >}} weights were released on {{< var design.s1.oews_release >}}, after the formation date of {{< var design.formation >}} and inside the return window, and its O*NET {{< var vintage.onet.primary >}} task links also postdate formation, although clarification C-74 in PAP §11 records that their task text is identical to that of {{< var vintage.onet.r32 >}} (@sec-app-deviations). R32 rebuilds the index from inputs public at formation (OEWS {{< var vintage.oews.r32 >}}, O*NET {{< var vintage.onet.r32 >}}) and gives an H5 slope of {{< var rob.r32.h5.estimate >}} pp per standard deviation (interval {{< var rob.r32.h5.ci_lo >}} to {{< var rob.r32.h5.ci_hi >}}, p = {{< var rob.r32.h5.p >}}) and an H5b slope of {{< var rob.r32.h5b.estimate >}} (interval {{< var rob.r32.h5b.ci_lo >}} to {{< var rob.r32.h5b.ci_hi >}}, p = {{< var rob.r32.h5b.p >}}); R1, on OEWS {{< var vintage.oews.r1 >}}, is look-ahead (@sec-robustness). R32 is a market row only, so no RQ2 correlation exists under strictly real-time inputs.

The seal kept code from reading industry returns dated on or after {{< var design.seal_date >}} until the protocol was tagged ({{< var pap.tag >}}, {{< var pap.date >}}). It cannot remove what the researchers, or the language model assisting them, know from public commentary about broad market moves since then. The protection is procedural: the confirmatory test, its exposure vector, its frozen null values and its script were fixed before any post-seal return was read, and Design A is exploratory for this reason (@sec-app-disclosures). Choices made before the tag were made with that general knowledge, and no procedure can show that it left them untouched.

The H6 talk index counts filers whose 10-K filings EDGAR full-text search returns for a quoted phrase. Its matching semantics are those the SEC implemented on the retrieval date, which this paper does not control; the case, whitespace and hyphen rules bind only the secondary measure. Each filer's FF49 industry is its current SIC from the EDGAR submissions file retrieved at {{< var h6.vintage.submissions_retrieved_utc >}}, applied to every filing year, so both inputs are fixed at retrieval rather than in the filing year (@sec-markets). The secondary measure, built on downloaded text, needed a data-integrity correction after results were seen: two truncated 10-K primary documents were fetched again, a correction to input data only, logged as deviation D-1 in PAP §11 (@sec-app-deviations). H6 is exploratory, and its sensitivity to single industries is the post-result leave-one-industry-out diagnostic (PAP §11 D-3; exploratory; not a decision; @tbl-diag-h6-influence).
